value: One row is one numbered schema migration that has been applied to this database, with the wall-clock time it was applied.
justification: Builder schema.sql:3-7 declares version INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, a true rowid alias with no SQLite nullability caveat. The two open uniqueness subjects are accidental. name is a human description, not declared UNIQUE; nothing prevents two migrations sharing wording. applied_at is DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP and is written by schema.sql:189-190, which inserts both versions in a single script run: a fresh initialisation from README.md:24 (sqlite3 ... < schema.sql) can give both rows the same second, since CURRENT_TIMESTAMP has one-second resolution and no UNIQUE is declared. Today's two rows differ (21:13:02 vs 00:19:00 next day) only because 0001 and 0002 were applied hours apart. Scope is invariant, not historical: every write is INSERT OR IGNORE (schema.sql:189-190, migrations/0002_source_rankings.sql:25-26) and no statement anywhere UPDATEs the table, so a version never holds different content over time - version 1 is always 'initial reference index schema'. version -> (name, applied_at) holds in every legal state. applied_at being instance-local is a portability property, not a scope one.

value: One row is one named local catalog or intake family from which source rows were imported into this index.
justification: Builder schema.sql:27-33 declares id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and catalog_key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE; the packet confirms both qualify. Both open uniqueness subjects are 2-row artifacts. kind is a classifier ('local-source-family', 'local-reference-family') - a category is meant to be shared by many catalogs, and sources.catalog_id (schema.sql:38) points at id, never at kind. note is free prose with DEFAULT '', so two catalogs with no note would collide. The flagged '[] (constant column) -> local_db_path' 2NF violation is likewise a snapshot artifact: both intakes happen to have landed in the same file (.local/meta/reference-index/reference-index.sqlite), which is exactly why the column exists as a per-catalog path rather than a constant. Scope is current-state: local_db_path is an environment-dependent local filesystem path in a directory README.md:1-3 declares 'intentionally local-only and ignored by Git', so catalog_key -> local_db_path describes the present checkout, not a universal fact. Identity (catalog_key) is stable; the path is not.

value: One row is the current applicability judgement of one source under one named ranking scope: its score, the reason for it, and when it was ranked.
justification: Builder migrations/0002_source_rankings.sql:3-11 (mirrored at schema.sql:92-100) declares PRIMARY KEY (source_id, scope) with both parts NOT NULL. source_id alone is observed unique only because all 40 rows carry scope='applicability', the column DEFAULT - measured: SELECT scope, count(*) returns one group, applicability|40. The composite PK exists precisely to admit further scopes, so source_id alone is the textbook accidental key, and the '[] (constant column) -> scope' 2NF flag is the same snapshot artifact refuted by that PK. reason is a free-text justification sentence, distinct across 40 rows by writing style alone; nothing declares it unique and two sources can share a rationale. The flagged 3NF violations reason -> score and reason -> ranked_at are downstream artifacts of that accident, not defects. Scope is current-state, not historical: PK (source_id, scope) admits exactly one row per scope, so a re-rank overwrites score/reason/ranked_at in place and ranked_at timestamps the present judgement - there is no history dimension in the key.

subject: model
value: One row is the extracted plain-text body of one source's local copy, held as a 1:1 private extension of that source.
justification: Builder schema.sql:87-90 declares source_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES sources(id) ON DELETE CASCADE. That is simultaneously the key and the foreign key, so the relation has no identity of its own: it is a 1:1 payload extension carrying the private extracted text out of the sources row. The single open uniqueness subject, text, is accidental. text is the payload, never declared unique, and two sources can legitimately hold identical extracted text - the same paper mirrored under two source_keys, or a duplicated local PDF - which the CASCADE-only relationship does nothing to prevent. Its uniqueness across 18 rows is a property of today's corpus. Scope is current-state: proposal:476-477 makes extracted text an import artifact of the current local copy (scanner req 3, 'import rows into sources and source_text'), refreshed on re-import, and proposal:38-44 keeps it local-only alongside local paths and hashes. No atomicity candidate was flagged and none is warranted: text is one document body, one value that is merely long.

subject: *all-unruled*
justification: 40 rows across 17 columns yield 125 FDs and 27 unruled determinants — the relation is describing its own sparsity. Six columns are blank in the majority: catalog_table/catalog_pk 35/40, uri/license 31/40, revision 26/40, sha256/citation 22/40; visibility is constant. Crucially, uri, sha256 and citation are unique wherever populated (9/9, 18/18, 18/18), and title (40/40) and local_path (39/40) are free-text near-keys. Every composite in the sample contains at least one such column, so each FD is carried by the same mechanism: unique non-blank values, plus a large blank group agreeing on other blanks. None of these determinants names an entity that owns the listed attributes; they are near-keys and default collapse. Only the DDL-declared constraints — id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and source_key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE — are enforced by the DBMS and therefore hold over every future row. The authoritative schema at Penrose-Wallpaper/.local/meta/reference-index/schema.sql declares no other uniqueness, and source_catalogs shows the two catalogs are dated intake batches, not classifications.

subject: author
justification: author yields 26 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.65); only 7 groups have more than one row. It holds because all three targets are near-constant: catalog_id is 1 in 35/40 rows, catalog_table is '' in 35/40, revision is '' in 26/40. The only non-empty revisions inside a repeated author are 'web capture' (Simon Tatham x5) and 'local master snapshot' (OPENRNDR x2) -- those record which import batch fetched the rows, not something the author owns; a person does not own a catalog id or a capture revision. author is not even a clean entity key here: 'IMAGINARY gGmbH' and 'IMAGINARY gGmbH / Christian Stussak' are separate free-text strings for overlapping entities.

subject: author,catalog_pk,uri
justification: A composite of an author name, an external catalog primary-key value and a URL, yielding 32 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.80) with only 4 testing groups. uri is '' in 31/40 rows and catalog_pk is '' in 35/40, so the composite is close to author alone plus a handful of unique URLs. Nothing named here owns a citation string or a file hash: the hash belongs to the source identified by source_key. In sources, 35/40 rows have catalog_table='' and catalog_pk='', 31/40 have uri='' and license='', 26/40 have revision='', and 22/40 have citation='' and sha256=''. An empty-string group is the absence of a value, not a shared value, so agreement inside it is not evidence of ownership.

subject: author,license,resource_type,text_path
justification: 39 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.97) -- a near-key with exactly one testing group of two rows. It contains text_path, a filesystem path with 26 distinct values in 40 rows. The single repeated group is sources 4 and 7 (both 'Chris van Tienhoven', pdf-set, same extracted-text directory), and they agree on local_path only because that local_path is a shared directory. A bundle of author, licence, media kind and a text path is not a thing that owns a storage location.

subject: author,resource_type,uri,year
justification: 38 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.95) with two testing groups of two rows each. uri is '' in 31/40 rows and year is NULL in 10/40, so this four-column composite is a near-key that determines text_path by almost never repeating. A (person, media kind, URL, year) tuple is not an entity that owns an extracted-text path.

subject: author,text_path,year
justification: 38 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.95), two testing groups. This is the previous determinant with uri and resource_type swapped, and it is the same artifact: text_path already has 26 distinct values in 40 rows, so adding author and year makes the combination nearly unique. resource_type is a property of the source (id/source_key), and nothing here names that source.

subject: author,uri,year
justification: 37 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.93), three testing groups. uri is '' in 31/40 rows, so on the 31 empty-uri rows this is just author,year; the 9 non-empty URIs are almost all distinct. citation and sha256 belong to the source row itself -- the builder's scanner requirement is 'a source hash matches the imported catalog hash', keyed by the source, not by a (person, URL, year) tuple.

subject: author,year
justification: 34 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.85), six testing groups. The target catalog_pk is '' in 35/40 rows, and the five non-empty values ('231'..'235') each occur exactly once, so every group is either ''->'' or a singleton. An author and a publication year cannot own a primary-key value inside an external catalog table. In sources, 35/40 rows have catalog_table='' and catalog_pk='', 31/40 have uri='' and license='', 26/40 have revision='', and 22/40 have citation='' and sha256=''. An empty-string group is the absence of a value, not a shared value, so agreement inside it is not evidence of ownership.

subject: catalog_id,catalog_pk,license,uri,year
justification: A five-column composite of bookkeeping fields yielding 33 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.82). Four of the five columns are dominated by one value (catalog_id=1 in 35/40, catalog_pk='' in 35/40, license='' in 31/40, uri='' in 31/40), so the dependency is carried by whichever column happens to be non-empty. Note it claims to determine revision while also being determined alongside it in a sibling candidate -- the mark of mutual near-uniqueness, not of ownership. In sources, 35/40 rows have catalog_table='' and catalog_pk='', 31/40 have uri='' and license='', 26/40 have revision='', and 22/40 have citation='' and sha256=''. An empty-string group is the absence of a value, not a shared value, so agreement inside it is not evidence of ownership.

subject: catalog_id,catalog_pk,revision,uri,year
justification: 31 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.78) from five bookkeeping columns. On the 30 rows where catalog_id=1 and catalog_pk='' and revision='' and uri='' this reduces to year alone, and the remaining rows are individually distinctive. Counts, ids, revisions and years do not identify anything that could own a citation or a content hash.

subject: catalog_id,catalog_table,revision,uri,year
justification: 31 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.78). catalog_table takes only two values ('' in 35/40, 'documents' in 5) and catalog_id only two (1 in 35/40), so this composite carries almost no information beyond uri and year; it separates rows by chance, not by naming an entity. citation and sha256 are attributes of the source identified by source_key.

subject: catalog_pk
justification: catalog_pk yields 6 distinct groups over 40 rows, but 35 of those rows sit in the single '' group and the five non-empty values ('231','232','233','234','235') each occur exactly once. So the dependency is 35 rows of ''->'' plus five singletons -- it is never actually tested. The direction is also backwards: catalog_pk is a primary-key value *inside* a catalog table, so the table identifies the pk, not the reverse. The real external identity is (catalog_id, catalog_table, catalog_pk) taken together.

subject: catalog_pk,resource_type,revision,uri
justification: 31 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.78). Three of the four columns are empty on most rows (catalog_pk 35/40, revision 26/40, uri 31/40), so this is mostly resource_type plus whatever single column is populated. A composite of a foreign pk fragment, a media-kind label and a capture revision is not an entity that owns a citation or a sha256.

subject: catalog_pk,resource_type,uri,year
justification: 36 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.90) with only three testing groups covering seven rows. It is a near-key built from three mostly-empty or near-constant columns plus year (NULL in 10/40). Claiming it owns citation, sha256 and text_path at once is the giveaway: a genuine owner determines a coherent attribute set, whereas a near-key determines everything.

subject: catalog_pk,resource_type,year
justification: 32 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.80). The target revision is '' in 26/40 rows, and catalog_pk is '' in 35/40, so most groups are (''-pk, type, year) -> ''. revision records how a copy was obtained ('web capture', 'local master snapshot') -- import-batch provenance of the source row, not something a media kind and a year determine.

subject: catalog_table,resource_type,revision,uri,year
justification: 36 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.90), three testing groups covering seven rows. catalog_table has two values and is '' in 35/40 rows; revision and uri are empty in most rows. This is a near-key assembled from bookkeeping columns, and like its sibling it claims citation, sha256 and text_path simultaneously -- the signature of sparsity rather than of an entity.

subject: catalog_table,revision,year
justification: The most-tested composite in this relation (24 distinct groups over 40 rows, 0.60, 9 testing groups covering 25 rows) and still an artifact: the target catalog_pk is '' in 35/40 rows, so those 25 tested rows are almost entirely ''->''. The five non-empty catalog_pk values are unique. A table name, a capture revision and a year do not own a primary-key value in an external catalog.

subject: citation
justification: citation yields 19 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.47), which looks well-supported until the composition is measured: all 22 rows with citation='' also have catalog_pk='', catalog_table='', revision='', sha256='' and uri='' -- verified directly. So the dependency is 22 rows of ''->'' plus 18 citation strings (e.g. 'arXiv:2407.05359v1') that each occur exactly once. There is not a single group in which a real citation repeats. citation is a free-text bibliographic display string, near-unique by construction, and the proposal treats it as a publishable attribute of a source, not as its identity; the identity is source_key.

subject: id -> author,catalog_id,catalog_pk,catalog_table,citation,license,local_path,resource_type,revision,sha256,source_key,text_path,title,uri,year
justification: Declared PRIMARY KEY in the authoritative schema.sql. Its determination is DBMS-enforced, so it holds over every future row rather than over these 40 — the one case where non-repetition proves intent instead of signalling a near-key. The surrogate row identity owns every source attribute.

subject: local_path
justification: 39 distinct groups over 40 rows (0.97) -- a near-key with exactly one repeated value. That repetition disproves the reading rather than supporting it: '.local/geometry/projective-euclidean/chris-van-tienhoven' is a *directory* shared by two genuinely different sources (id 4 'cvt-selected-eqf-notes' and id 7 'cvt-conic-cubic-encyclopedias', different titles and source_keys), so local_path is a storage container, not a per-source identity. The six attributes it 'determines' are simply the columns on which those two rows happen to agree -- and four of them (catalog_pk, catalog_table, citation, license) agree only by both being ''. The proposal also marks local_path as private data to be redacted from published reports, i.e. an attribute of the source, not its key.

subject: resource_type -> catalog_id
justification: The direction is backwards from ownership: catalog_id is an FK to a dated intake batch (source_catalogs rows 'intake-2026-06-05' and 'etc-triangle-centers-2026-06-05'), and a file's format label cannot determine which batch it arrived in. It holds only because catalog 2 is a single 5-row intake whose five resource_type values happen not to recur among catalog 1's 35 rows. One ETC pdf breaks it.

subject: sha256 -> catalog_pk,catalog_table,citation,revision,uri
justification: Blank in 22 of 40 rows and unique across all 18 populated ones. The FD is carried entirely by that split: 18 unique hashes plus 22 blanks whose catalog_pk, catalog_table, citation, revision and uri are themselves mostly blank. A content hash identifies bytes; it does not own provenance metadata.

subject: source_key -> author,catalog_id,catalog_pk,catalog_table,citation,id,license,local_path,resource_type,revision,sha256,text_path,title,uri,year
justification: Declared TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE in schema.sql and used as the stable natural handle for a source (it is the join surface in source_fts and the public views). Enforced by the DBMS, so unlike title its uniqueness is a constraint on the modelled world, not an observation over 40 rows.

subject: title -> author,catalog_id,catalog_pk,catalog_table,citation,id,license,local_path,resource_type,revision,sha256,source_key,text_path,uri,year
justification: 40/40 distinct, exactly like source_key — but nothing in the schema prevents two sources sharing a title, and this corpus already holds several near-duplicate captures of the same work. Free-text human labelling that happens not to collide is a near-key, not an owner.

subject: model
value: One row is one cited source identity - a paper, package, codebase, capture, or manual - together with the current local holding and public citation metadata recorded for it.
justification: Builder schema.sql:35-54 declares id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and source_key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE; the CLI sketch (proposal:461-462) addresses sources by source_key, never by descriptive columns. One mechanism disposes of five of the six open uniqueness subjects: they are artifacts of empty-string defaults. Measured over 40 rows: uri empty 31, license empty 31, catalog_table empty 35, sha256 empty 22, text_path empty 13, year NULL 10. So (author,license,resource_type,uri,year) effectively collapses to (author,resource_type,year), and the others likewise - they separate rows only because today's 40 authors and years happen to differ, and each becomes non-unique the moment two sources by one author share a year. title is separately accidental: DEFAULT '' means two untitled sources collide, and two editions or translations legitimately share a title. Scope is current-state: local_path, text_path and sha256 record the present local holding (proposal:84-90, 393-396), so source_key -> sha256 is a snapshot fact; the identity source_key and the public citation fields are the stable part.

subject: model
value: One row is one topic claim made by one code symbol's @pwref annotation: this symbol declares that it implements or depends on this topic.
justification: Builder schema.sql:80-85 declares PRIMARY KEY (symbol_id, topic_id) with both parts NOT NULL and both FKs ON DELETE CASCADE. This is the associative relation that already normalises the many-to-many between symbols and topics, and proposal:215 confirms the intended cardinality: 'Multiple tags are allowed on one symbol', so neither column alone can be a key. annotation_text is the literal '@pwref <slug>' text that produced the claim - payload, not identity - and the PK implies at most one claim per (symbol, topic) pair, so a symbol tagging the same topic twice collapses to one row. Scope is per-build: scanner requirement 5 (proposal:479) is 'Replace scanned code_symbols and symbol_topics rows for the current scan', so both this relation and the code_symbols surrogate ids it references are regenerated wholesale each scan; nothing here survives a rescan by identity. The table holds 0 rows (the scanner has not been run here), which leaves no observed dependencies but does not weaken a model read from DDL plus the annotation contract.

subject: model
value: One row is one alternate name that resolves to exactly one canonical topic.
justification: Builder schema.sql:21-25 declares alias TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY (topic_id, alias). The UNIQUE is global, not per-topic, so {alias} is already a superkey and the declared composite PK properly contains it: (topic_id, alias) is a superkey but not minimal, hence not a candidate key. The single intended key is therefore alias alone, and alias -> topic_id is the intended dependency. That is exactly the semantics proposal:218 requires - 'Aliases are query/import conveniences, not code annotations' - an alias must resolve to one topic or it cannot serve as an import convenience, while proposal:511 requires code to use the canonical slug rather than an alias. The packet agrees: the only observed UCC is ['alias'], and the declared constraint list qualifies alias as a key. This relation is also the design's own demonstration that a repeating fact (a topic has several names) belongs in a child relation rather than a delimited column. Scope invariant: aliases are curated vocabulary, and alias -> topic_id holds in every legal state.

subject: locator
justification: One citation pointer into one source, and a declared PRIMARY KEY component (schema.sql:64), all three parts NOT NULL. The schema's own mechanism for 'this topic cites several places in one source' is therefore several rows, not a child relation - and a child topic_source_locators would be actively wrong, because relevance, relationship, applies_to and note are per-locator under that key and decomposition would lose them. Values are prose region references ('Chapter 1', 'Sections 2.2-2.14', 'whole capture', 'README and source tree'), and proposal:531 makes breadth a warning, not a failure: 'A locator is broad, such as an entire chapter or file.' locator='' (33/54 rows) is a legitimate key value meaning the whole source. Exactly one row of 54 (topic 38 / source 23) semicolon-joins five Shinagawa coefficient filenames; that is a data-entry violation of the intended key shape, remediated by splitting it into five rows within topic_sources, not evidence of a designed repeating group.

subject: note
justification: One free-text annotation describing why this source supports this topic - a single prose sentence, e.g. 'Numeric barycentric package for point, line, conic, curve, and transformation construction.' The ','_list flag fires on ordinary English enumeration inside one sentence, not on a delimited value list: the commas are grammar, and no reader or query ever splits the column. It is declared TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '' (schema.sql:63) as optional payload, is never parsed, and appears in v_topic_sources (schema.sql:119) as a single reported field. The design also forbids the thing that would make it a repeating group: proposal:626 'No topic-per-source tags' and proposal:625 'No long quotations in SQLite.'

subject: applies_to,topic_id
justification: 32 distinct groups over 54 rows (0.59). Both columns are pure categorisation: applies_to has 4 values and topic_id is the link's own key fragment. The target relationship is 'reference' in 49/54 rows (0.91), so almost any grouping satisfies this by default. The builder makes relationship a per-link argument, not a function of the topic and platform: 'link-topic <topic> <source> --relevance primary --relationship api-contract --applies-to web'.

subject: locator
justification: 17 distinct groups over 54 rows (0.31), and the three groups that actually test the dependency are locator='' (33 rows), 'whole capture' (5 rows) and 'Penrose half-tile sections' (2 rows). The 33-row group is the absence of a locator, not a shared locator. Combined with relationship being 'reference' in 49/54 rows, nothing is being measured. A locator is a free-text pointer into a source ('orx-fft and visual extension modules'); the proposal even lists 'a locator is broad, such as an entire chapter or file' as a warning condition. It cannot own the license-bearing relationship kind.

subject: locator,relevance,topic_id
justification: 46 distinct groups over 54 rows (0.85) with only 8 testing groups covering 16 rows. (topic_id, locator) are two of the three declared primary-key columns, so this is the key minus source_id -- a near-key by construction. It determines applies_to because it barely repeats, not because a (topic, citation-locator, relevance) tuple owns a platform label.

subject: note
justification: note has 53 distinct values in 54 rows (0.98) -- a free-text annotation that is effectively unique per row. It 'determines' applies_to, relationship and relevance the way a primary key would: by almost never repeating. This is the textbook free-text near-key artifact, and the single repeated note gives one two-row group of support.

subject: relationship,relevance,topic_id
justification: 44 distinct groups over 54 rows (0.81), 9 testing groups. relevance has 3 values and relationship 3 (49/54 of them 'reference'), so the separating power comes almost entirely from topic_id -- and a topic does not own the platform a citation applies to. The builder supplies --relevance, --relationship and --applies-to as three independent per-link arguments, which is exactly the opposite of two of them determining the third.

subject: source_id
justification: The builder settles this against the data. The proposal states the index records the relationship type 'for each topic-source link', enumerating reference / api-contract / inspiration / comparison / derived / dependency as properties of the link, and the CLI takes them at link time: 'link-topic <topic> <source> --relevance primary --relationship api-contract --applies-to web'. Both columns live on the junction table with DEFAULTs ('reference', 'cross') precisely so each link can differ; if a source owned them they would sit in sources. The measurement corroborates rather than contradicts this: 40 distinct source_id over 54 rows (0.74) leaves only 11 testing groups, and the agreement inside them is explained by the modal values -- relationship is 'reference' in 49/54 rows and applies_to is 'math' in 41/54, because this corpus is mostly mathematics papers. A source that is cited as a reference by one topic and adapted ('derived') by another would break this immediately.

subject: model
value: One row is one curated claim that a given topic is supported by a given source at one specific locator within it, qualified by relevance, relationship, and platform applicability.
justification: Builder schema.sql:56-68 declares PRIMARY KEY (topic_id, source_id, locator), all three NOT NULL, plus CHECKs constraining relevance, relationship and applies_to to closed vocabularies. The critical open subject is the observed UCC (source_id, topic_id). It is accidental, and it is the designed-in trap: measured, all 54 rows have 54 distinct (topic_id, source_id) pairs, so the pair is unique today - but the author deliberately put locator in the key precisely so one topic may cite several distinct places in one source with different relevance or notes. Accepting (source_id, topic_id) would forbid a legal future state the DDL explicitly permits. (note, topic_id) is likewise accidental: note is optional prose with DEFAULT '', so two links from one topic with no note collide. The flagged 2NF/3NF violations with note or source_id as determinant are artifacts of those accidental UCCs under the observed key basis, not real defects. Scope invariant: proposal:155-158 makes this the relation where 'the claim that a source supports a topic lives' - curated editorial state, not a snapshot or a regenerated artifact.

subject: summary
justification: One short prose description of the topic, e.g. 'Penrose rhomb substitution and rendering family.' or 'Barycentric and trilinear coordinate functions, conics, curves, triangle and quadrilateral operations.' The ','_list flag fires on ordinary English enumeration within a single sentence; the commas are grammar, not a delimiter. It is declared TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '' (schema.sql:14) as optional descriptive payload, is never split or parsed, and no query or view in schema.sql:110-187 does anything with it but report it. Decisively, this schema already demonstrates how it normalises a genuinely repeating fact about a topic: topic_aliases (schema.sql:21-25) for multiple names, symbol_topics and topic_sources for multiple links. A repeating group in summary would be inconsistent with that pattern.

subject: id -> domain,public,slug,summary,title
justification: Declared id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY in builder schema.sql:9-19. Surrogate identity of the topic entity; owns every topic attribute by construction, invariant under any number of future rows. Matches the standing approved uniqueness/id=intended decision.

subject: slug -> domain,id,public,summary,title
justification: Declared slug TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE in schema.sql:9-19 and used as the semantic key throughout: the <domain>.<system>.<name> vocabulary that @pwref code annotations name and topic_sources/topic_aliases resolve against. A real entity owning real attributes, enforced by DDL rather than by row count. Matches standing uniqueness/slug=intended.

subject: summary -> domain,id,public,slug,title
justification: One line of free prose describing the topic, DEFAULT '' and unconstrained; distinct in all 52 current rows purely because each was written separately. The empty-string default alone shows repetition is permitted. Near-key, not an owner. Matches standing uniqueness/summary=accidental.

subject: title -> domain,id,public,slug,summary
justification: Free-text display label with no uniqueness constraint; 52/52 distinct only in the current rows. Two topics in different domains could share a title and nothing in the schema prevents it. A near-key holding by rarity, not an owner. Matches standing uniqueness/title=accidental.

subject: model
value: One row is one canonical topic in the project's reference vocabulary - the durable subject that @pwref code annotations name and that sources are linked to.
justification: Builder schema.sql:9-19 declares id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and slug TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, with CHECKs on status and public. slug is the semantic key throughout: proposal:222-227 fixes the <domain>.<system>.<specific-topic> form, proposal:214 says the @pwref tag 'contains only a canonical slug', and proposal:511 requires annotations to use the canonical slug, not an alias. Both open uniqueness subjects are accidental. summary is DEFAULT '', so two topics with no summary collide immediately; title has no UNIQUE and is a human label that two topics in different domains can legitimately share. Both are unique across today's 52 rows only because each was hand-written once. The '[] (constant column) -> status' 2NF flag is a snapshot artifact refuted by the DDL itself: CHECK (status IN ('active','retired')) makes 'retired' legal, all 52 rows merely happen to be active today, and proposal:512 relies on retirement ('A retired topic is not used in code'). Scope invariant, unlike source_rankings: status is a lifecycle flag on a durable vocabulary entry, and slug -> (domain, title, summary) holds in every legal state.
